analysis.one_liner: Strips ocean shipping lines of their exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Ocean shipping lines currently operate under a federal exemption that lets agreements among carriers escape antitrust enforcement. This bill repeals that exemption, applies normal antitrust laws to ocean common carriers, and lets the Federal Maritime Commission submit written analyses to the Justice Department about proposed mergers in the industry. It preserves the separate exemption for agreements about collectively bargained worker benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that ship goods by sea — importers, exporters, farmers, retailers, and manufacturers — and ultimately consumers, since ocean freight rates feed into the prices of imported and exported goods. Stronger antitrust review could also slow further consolidation among the small number of giant carriers that control most container shipping.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provision of federal shipping law (46 U.S.C. §40307) that exempts ocean common carriers from the antitrust laws, so carrier agreements would face normal competition rules [S2] [S3].
Keeps antitrust laws from applying only to assessment agreements covering collectively bargained fringe benefit obligations, protecting the narrow piece tied to workers' benefits [S2] [S3].

Authorizes the Federal Maritime Commission to analyze and submit written views to the Justice Department's Antitrust Division on mergers and acquisitions of common carriers and marine terminal operators, including effects on competition and on America's trade position [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The major ocean shipping lines — largely foreign-owned carriers and the alliances they form — which would lose legal protection for coordinated pricing and capacity decisions and could face antitrust suits and closer merger scrutiny.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ocean shipping lines and their alliances

drawbacks.text: The exemption exists to let carriers coordinate schedules and share vessel space, which the industry argues lowers costs and keeps regular service running; repealing it could disrupt those arrangements and, its defenders say, raise costs or reduce service, especially to smaller ports [S2] [S3].

The bill gives the Federal Maritime Commission a formal advisory role in merger reviews without changing the Justice Department's ultimate authority, so its practical effect depends on how actively the agencies use it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — ending an industry-specific carve-out from the antitrust laws — would subject a handful of huge carriers to the same competition rules other industries face, which shippers and consumers have clear reason to want, particularly after freight rate spikes. The honest cost side is that shipping alliances argue their coordination produces efficiencies that ordinary competition might not replace, and the bill does nothing itself to lower rates; it only restores legal tools that must then be used. On balance the bill is modest, targeted, and tilted toward shippers and consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Transportation and Infrastructure committees, sent to a transportation subcommittee the next day, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Costa introduced the bill on March 22, 2023, joined by four cosponsors (three Democrats and one Republican) [S3] [S4].
The Speaker referred it to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee [S1] [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation; no committee or subcommittee action, hearing, or vote followed for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major ocean shipping carriers and their alliances, which kept their antitrust exemption intact for another Congress; American shippers and consumers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Jim Costa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the ocean carriers' antitrust exemption.

for.name: Reps. John Garamendi, Jimmy Panetta, Josh Harder, and Dusty Johnson
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties (3 Democrats, 1 Republican).

against.name: House Judiciary and Transportation and Infrastructure committees
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill in the roughly 21 months after referral, keeping it off the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but thin: the sponsor was a Democrat and the four cosponsors split 3-1 between Democrats and a Republican, and no chamber ever voted on it.

industries.industry: Ocean shipping lines and carrier alliances
industries.note: The bill repeals their exemption from antitrust laws, ending legal cover for agreements that coordinate pricing, capacity, and scheduling across the small group of carriers that dominates container shipping. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against shippers and consumers who bear the freight rates embedded in prices.

The bill would subject their mergers and acquisitions to written antitrust analysis by the Federal Maritime Commission, adding scrutiny. The burden is procedural rather than a direct ban on any practice.

industries.industry: U.S. exporters and importers (agriculture, retail, manufacturing)
industries.note: These businesses would gain a legal tool to challenge carrier coordination that they blame for high and volatile freight rates, a cost that ultimately reaches consumers.
